name: Dust of Snow by Robert Frost

scenes.animation: A gloomy man trudges through a winter garden under a grey cloud. A crow on a hemlock branch shakes it, and a puff of snow drops on his head. The grey cloud pops like a bubble.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Snow on your head, and suddenly you're happy? I'd be annoyed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That tiny moment is the whole poem. Dust of Snow, by Robert Frost.

scenes.animation: The poem's scene builds step by step: a hemlock tree, a black crow on a branch, a sprinkle of white 'dust of snow' falling onto the poet. A mood meter slides from 'rued' to 'saved'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poet is having a bad day. A crow on a hemlock tree shakes down a dust of snow on him.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This small act changes his mood and saves some part of a day he had rued, or regretted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The whole poem is just one sentence, split into two short stanzas.

scenes.animation: Two info cards flip over. 'Crow: often a sign of bad omen or sorrow'. 'Hemlock: a poisonous plant, sign of gloom'. A lightbulb glows: 'Even these brought joy'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why a crow? Couldn't Frost pick a cute parrot?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's the point. The crow and the hemlock usually suggest sorrow and gloom. Yet they bring a happy change.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So, even ordinary or unpleasant things in nature can lift our spirits.

scenes.animation: Device tags stick onto the poem: 'Symbolism', 'Rhyme scheme: abab', 'Alliteration: has given my heart'. Snowflakes float around each tag.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Key devices: symbolism, in the crow, hemlock and snow, and a simple a b a b rhyme scheme.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The snow itself stands for a fresh, cheerful moment.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So a tiny thing can change a whole mood?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Frost shows that nature can heal us, even in a small, unexpected moment.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. What is the significance of the crow and the hemlock?' Answer bullets build: usual negative symbols, used to show a positive change. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: why did Frost choose a crow and a hemlock tree instead of a lovelier bird or tree?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: say they usually suggest bad luck and sorrow, and explain that the poet shows even these can bring joy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: always explain what 'rued' means. It is a word examiners expect you to know.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A second question: how did the poet's mood change? Say it went from sad and regretful to fresh and hopeful.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a crow and a snowflake: '1. Crow shakes snow on poet', '2. His mood changes; day is saved', '3. Crow and hemlock = gloom, yet bring joy'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a crow shakes snow from a hemlock tree onto the poet.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: this small moment changes his mood and saves his day.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: even symbols of gloom can bring joy.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Okay, but next time the crow can just say hello.

name: Fire and Ice by Robert Frost

scenes.animation: Zippy sits on a globe, holding a debate placard. One half of the globe blazes red, the other half freezes blue. A scoreboard reads 'Fire vs Ice'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Big debate: will the world end in fire or ice?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Robert Frost weighed in, in just nine lines. His poem is Fire and Ice.

scenes.animation: Two crowds appear: one yelling 'Fire!', the other 'Ice!'. The poet walks in, nods toward Fire, then towards Ice. Labels appear: 'Fire = desire', 'Ice = hatred'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some say the world will end in fire, some say in ice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poet says that from what he has tasted of desire, he favours fire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But if the world had to perish twice, he knows enough of hate to say ice would also do.

scenes.animation: Fire becomes a greedy hand grabbing coins and land; ice becomes a cold, frozen heart. Both slowly spread across the globe.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So he's not talking about a volcano and an ice age?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Only on the surface. Fire stands for desire and greed, which spreads fast. Ice stands for hatred, cold and rigid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The message: human emotions like greed and hatred can destroy the world.

scenes.animation: Device tags stick to the poem: 'Symbolism', 'Understatement: would suffice', 'Rhyme'. A small snowflake sits on the word 'suffice' with a knowing wink.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Devices: symbolism in fire and ice, and a clever understatement at the end.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Saying ice 'would suffice' makes hatred sound calm, which makes it even more frightening.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why do both sound so reasonable?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because Frost speaks calmly, like a casual chat, about the end of the world. That calm tone makes the warning stronger.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. What do fire and ice stand for?' Two columns build: 'Fire: desire, greed, lust' and 'Ice: hatred, indifference'. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: what do fire and ice symbolise, and what is the poet's message?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: fire is desire, ice is hatred, and both can destroy the world if left unchecked.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: quote 'would suffice' and call it understatement. It earns you the device mark.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Another likely question asks why the poet first favours fire. Say he has tasted desire and knows how fast it spreads.

scenes.animation: Recap board with flame and ice-cube icons: '1. World may end in fire or ice', '2. Fire = desire; ice = hatred', '3. Human emotions can destroy the world'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: people debate whether the world will end in fire or ice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: fire stands for desire, and ice for hatred.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: both emotions have the power to destroy the world.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the real danger is us, not the weather.

name: A Tiger in the Zoo by Leslie Norris

scenes.animation: A school trip at a zoo. Kids with ice creams wave at a tiger pacing in a concrete cell. Zippy waves too; the tiger ignores him with a cold stare.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is he so grumpy? He gets free meals!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Would you trade freedom for free meals? That question drives A Tiger in the Zoo, by Leslie Norris.

scenes.animation: The tiger stalks the length of his cage; his velvet paws are quiet but his eyes burn. The label 'quiet rage' glows red near him.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The tiger stalks the length of his cage in quiet rage. His power is hidden behind bars.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He ignores the visitors. His strength and beauty are wasted here.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Quiet rage? That sounds like me when the canteen runs out of samosas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Close! He is furious but powerless. His rage has nowhere to go, so it stays silent.

scenes.animation: Split-screen: the tiger lurking in long grass near a water hole; then snarling at the edge of a village, where cartoon villagers peek from huts. The cage shrinks into the corner.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poet imagines where he should be: lurking in shadow in the long grass, near the water hole, hunting plump deer.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He should be snarling around houses at the jungle's edge, baring his white fangs and claws, terrorising the village.

scenes.animation: Night at the zoo. Headlights of patrolling cars sweep past. The tiger lifts his head and stares with his brilliant eyes at the brilliant stars; the stars seem far away.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: At night, he hears the patrolling cars and stares with his brilliant eyes at the brilliant stars.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Sounds like he's dreaming of home.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. The contrast between cage and jungle shows the pain of captivity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He cannot reach the stars or the jungle. The poem quietly asks whether zoos are fair to such animals.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. How does the poet contrast the tiger in the zoo and in the wild?' Two columns build: 'Cage: quiet rage, ignoring visitors' and 'Wild: lurking, hunting, snarling'. Device tags pop: 'Alliteration', 'Imagery', 'Enjambment'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: contrast the tiger in the cage with the tiger in the wild.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: list what he does in each place, then state the theme: wild animals belong in freedom.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: note devices like alliteration in 'sliding through long grass' and repetition in 'brilliant eyes' and 'brilliant stars'.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a tiger icon: '1. In the zoo: quiet rage', '2. In the wild: lurking, hunting, powerful', '3. Theme: captivity vs freedom'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: in the zoo, the tiger paces his cage in quiet rage.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: in the wild, he would hunt freely and be feared.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the poem pleads for the freedom of wild animals.

name: How to Tell Wild Animals by Carolyn Wells

scenes.animation: Zippy holds a fake field guide titled 'Jungle Safety for Dummies'. A large tawny lion roars behind him; Zippy flips pages frantically.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: How do I know which animal is chasing me?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Carolyn Wells has a funny guide for that: How to Tell Wild Animals.

scenes.animation: A cartoon field guide opens. Page one: a tawny beast roars, labelled 'Asian Lion'. Page two: a tiger with black stripes on yellow, labelled 'Bengal Tiger'. Page three: a spotted cat pouncing, labelled 'Leopard'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If a large, tawny beast roars at you as you are dying, you'll know it is the Asian Lion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If a noble beast, yellow with black stripes, eats you, that's the Bengal Tiger.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If spots appear on a beast that leaps at you, it's the Leopard, and crying out won't help.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Hold on. Identifying an animal only when it eats you is not a great safety plan.

scenes.animation: More pages: a bear crushing a person in a hug; a smiling hyena; a crocodile shedding big fake tears; a chameleon that blends into a tree.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If a creature hugs you very, very hard, that's a Bear.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Hyena comes with a smile, and the Crocodile weeps tears as it eats you.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Chameleon has no ears and no wings, and you may not see it at all on a tree.

scenes.animation: Device tags stick on: 'Humour and irony', 'Poetic licence: dyin' / Lion', 'Alliteration: noble wild beast', 'Rhyme'. Zippy laughs so hard he falls off the page.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Wait, you only learn which animal it is once it has eaten you?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. That's the irony and the humour of the poem.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poet uses poetic licence too, writing 'dyin'' to rhyme with 'Lion'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She also plays with spelling, as in 'lept' and 'lep' for the Leopard, to keep the rhythm fun.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. What is the poetic licence in the poem?' Neo underlines 'dyin'' and 'Lion'. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: identify an example of poetic licence and explain the humour.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: explain that the poet bends grammar or spelling for rhyme and rhythm, as in 'dyin'' and 'Lion'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: say that the crocodile's tears refer to 'crocodile tears', meaning fake sorrow.

scenes.animation: Recap board with paw-print icons: '1. A humorous guide to wild animals', '2. Each animal identified by its dangerous trait', '3. Poetic licence, irony and rhyme'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the poem is a funny guide to identifying wild animals.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: each animal is known by the dangerous thing it does to you.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: look for humour, irony and poetic licence.

name: The Ball Poem by John Berryman

scenes.animation: A boy plays with a red ball along a street by a harbour. It bounces, bounces, then drops into the dark water with a plop. Zippy gasps.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Oh no. Quick, someone buy him another ball!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's exactly what the poet refuses to do. This is The Ball Poem, by John Berryman.

scenes.animation: The boy stands still, trembling, staring at the harbour where the ball sank. Memories of the ball in happier days float around him like bubbles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The boy loses his ball, and it drifts into the water. He stands rigid, trembling, staring at where it went.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The ball carried memories of his childhood days. Its loss is his first real experience of loss.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: It's just a ball, though. Why is he so upset?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because it is his, and it is gone forever. For a child, that feels huge. The poet respects that feeling.

scenes.animation: A passer-by holds out a coin; the poet gently stops his hand. A caption appears: 'Money is external'. The boy looks thoughtful.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why won't the poet just give him money?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because money is external. It can buy a new ball, but not the memories or the lesson.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The boy must learn the epistemology of loss, how to live with loss and stand up again.

scenes.animation: A growing-up animation: the boy gets slightly taller and older with each frame, carrying a little bag labelled 'responsibility'. Device tags appear: 'Symbolism: ball = childhood', 'Free verse'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The ball symbolises childhood and everything we lose as we grow.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The message: loss is part of life, and learning to accept it is part of growing up.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Every one of us will lose things. What matters is learning to stand up again.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Why doesn't the poet offer money to buy another ball?' Answer points build: money is external, lesson of loss, responsibility. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: why does the poet not offer the boy money for another ball?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: say that money cannot replace memories, and the boy must learn to accept loss and grow up.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: explain 'epistemology of loss' in simple words: understanding what it means to lose something.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a ball icon: '1. Boy loses his ball in the harbour', '2. Money is external', '3. Learn to accept loss and grow up'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a boy loses his ball in the harbour and is heartbroken.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the poet does not offer money, because money is external.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: learning to accept loss is part of growing up.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Still, I'm keeping my ball far from the harbour.

scenes.animation: A girl at a table surrounded by speech bubbles in brackets: '(Don't bite your nails, Amanda!)', '(Don't hunch your shoulders!)', '(Stop that sulking!)'. Zippy ducks under the barrage.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Whoa, that's a lot of instructions in one minute.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Welcome to Amanda!, by Robin Klein. The bracketed lines are the voice of her nagging mother.

scenes.animation: Amanda closes her eyes and turns into a mermaid in a languid, emerald sea. Then she becomes an orphan roaming bare-footed in a quiet street, drawing patterns in the soft dust.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Amanda escapes into her imagination. First, she is a mermaid in a languid, emerald sea.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Next, she is an orphan, roaming the streets barefoot, with golden silence and sweet freedom.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why would anyone want to be an orphan?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She doesn't really. She just wants silence and freedom, away from constant instructions.

scenes.animation: Amanda as Rapunzel in a tall tower, calm and alone. She sees no one coming and does not let down her hair. The mother's bracketed voice bounces off the tower wall.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then she is Rapunzel in a tower, so tranquil that she would never let down her bright hair.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The mother keeps nagging about homework, chocolate and her room, and ends by saying anyone would think she nagged at her.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: That last line is pure irony.

scenes.animation: Device tags stick on: 'Irony', 'Metaphor: mermaid, orphan, Rapunzel', 'Alliteration', 'Contrast of voices'. A caption appears: 'Children need freedom and space'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The message: too much nagging can push a child away. Children need freedom, space and understanding.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poem uses irony, metaphor and a contrast between the mother's voice and Amanda's thoughts.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the mom means well, but it backfires.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. The more she nags, the further Amanda drifts into her dreams.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Is Amanda sulking? Why does she imagine being a mermaid?' Answer points build: not sulking, daydreaming, longing for freedom. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: is Amanda really sulking? What do her daydreams show?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: she is not sulking but escaping; each daydream shows her longing for freedom and peace.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: say who speaks the lines in brackets. Many students miss that it is the mother.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a mermaid tail icon: '1. Mother nags; Amanda daydreams', '2. Mermaid, orphan, Rapunzel = freedom', '3. Children need space and understanding'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Amanda's mother nags her constantly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Amanda imagines being a mermaid, an orphan and Rapunzel, all symbols of freedom.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: children need freedom and understanding, not constant correction.

scenes.animation: Night. Potted trees inside a house slowly pull their roots from cracks in the veranda floor and inch toward the front door. Zippy stares in disbelief.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Are those trees moving out of the house? Did they not pay rent?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ha! This is The Trees, by Adrienne Rich. The trees are leaving the house for the forest.

scenes.animation: A bare forest outside: no birds, no insects, no shade. Inside, roots work to disengage from the veranda floor, leaves strain toward the glass, and twigs stiffen with effort.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Outside, the forest is empty, with no bird to sit on and no insect to hide in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Inside, roots work all night to free themselves, leaves strain toward the glass, and small twigs grow stiff with exertion.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Trees working all night? They should unionise.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ha! The poet makes them sound like living beings, struggling hard to escape.

scenes.animation: The poet sits by an open door writing long letters. The big boughs bend and shuffle toward the door like patients leaving a hospital. The moon breaks like a mirror as the trees move out.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The long-cramped boughs shuffle under the roof like newly discharged patients heading for the doors.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poet writes long letters and barely mentions the forest leaving the house. By morning, the moon is broken like a mirror.

scenes.animation: Two meanings unfold side by side: nature reclaiming land from humans, and a woman stepping out of a small house labelled 'limits'. Device tags pop: 'Personification', 'Simile', 'Symbolism'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So it's just about plants?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It works on two levels. Nature is breaking free from human control, and the trees can also stand for women breaking free from confinement.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Key devices: personification, similes like 'newly discharged patients', and symbolism.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. What does the poet mean by the forest being empty? What do the trees symbolise?' A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: why is the forest empty, and what do the trees symbolise?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: without trees, birds and insects have no home; the trees symbolise the urge for freedom.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: find the simile and the personification with their exact words.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Another likely question: why does the poet scarcely mention the trees leaving? Say that people often fail to notice changes in nature around them.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a tree icon: '1. Trees leave the house for the forest', '2. The empty forest needs them', '3. Symbol: nature and people breaking free'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the trees leave the house to return to the forest.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the forest is empty without them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the poem is about freedom, for nature and for people.

scenes.animation: A harbour city at dawn. A soft grey fog creeps in, and its edge slowly takes the shape of a giant, silent cat with paws. Zippy hides behind a lamp post.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, why is the fog shaped like a giant cat?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because Carl Sandburg imagined it that way. The poem is Fog, and it's only six lines long.

scenes.animation: The fog-cat pads in on little cat feet, sits on silent haunches looking over the harbour and city, then gets up and moves on, revealing the sunny city behind.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The fog comes on little cat feet, silently and suddenly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It sits looking over the harbour and the city on silent haunches, and then moves on.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: That's it? Six lines?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Six lines, but a complete picture. The fog arrives, rests and leaves, all without a sound.

scenes.animation: Side-by-side comparison chart: 'Cat: silent, sits, watches, leaves on its own' vs 'Fog: silent, settles, covers the city, lifts'. Tick marks connect each pair.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why a cat? Why not a slow elephant?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A cat moves silently, sits still and watches, then leaves whenever it likes. Fog behaves the same way.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This comparison runs through the whole poem, so it's called an extended metaphor.

scenes.animation: Device tags stick on: 'Extended metaphor', 'Personification', 'Free verse: no rhyme scheme'. A tiny cat tail flicks out of the last tag.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Fog is also personified, and the poem is in free verse, with no fixed rhyme or metre.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The message: nature can be quiet, mysterious and temporary.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Short and mysterious. Just like a cat.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Right. And like a cat, the fog does not stay long. It moves on when it chooses.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Which animal does the fog remind the poet of? How does the poet show it?' A 'Board Tip' sticker points at 'little cat feet'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: what animal does the poet compare the fog to, and how?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: name the cat and quote 'little cat feet' and 'silent haunches' as evidence.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: say 'extended metaphor', not simile. There is no 'like' or 'as' comparing fog to a cat.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a cat-paw icon in mist: '1. Fog comes silently on cat feet', '2. Sits over harbour and city, then moves on', '3. Extended metaphor; free verse'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the fog comes silently, like a cat.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: it sits over the harbour and city, then moves on.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the poem is an extended metaphor in free verse.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next foggy morning, I'm saying 'Here, kitty kitty.'

name: The Tale of Custard the Dragon by Ogden Nash

scenes.animation: A little white house. Belinda poses with her pets: a little black kitten, a little grey mouse, a little yellow dog, and a little pet dragon hiding behind them. Name tags pop: 'Ink', 'Blink', 'Mustard', 'Custard'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A kitten, a mouse, a dog and a dragon? That's one wild pet shop.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Meet Belinda and her pets in The Tale of Custard the Dragon, by Ogden Nash.

scenes.animation: Ink, Blink and Mustard strike brave poses. Custard trembles, and a caption appears: 'cries for a nice safe cage'. The others laugh at him.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Belinda was as brave as a barrel full of bears. Ink and Blink could chase lions down the stairs, and Mustard was as brave as a tiger in a rage.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But Custard was a cowardly dragon who cried for a nice safe cage. Everyone teased him.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A dragon that wants a safe cage? That's adorable.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And that's the joke. The poet uses funny similes to build up the others and knock Custard down.

scenes.animation: A pirate climbs in the window with pistols in both hands and a cutlass in his teeth. Belinda shouts for help, Mustard flees, Ink hides at the bottom of the house, and Blink dives into a mousehole.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One day a pirate climbs in through the window, with pistols in his hands and a cutlass between his teeth.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Belinda cries for help, and the so-called brave pets run and hide.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mustard runs with a terrified yelp, Ink trickles to the bottom of the household, and Blink hides in a mousehole.

scenes.animation: Custard leaps forward snorting, his tail clashing like iron in a dungeon. The pirate fires, misses, and Custard gobbles him up. Belinda hugs Custard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Custard jumps up, snorting like an engine, and gobbles the pirate up.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the coward was the only hero!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. But afterwards, the others still boast that they are braver, and Custard still cries for a nice safe cage.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Who is really brave in the poem? What is ironic?' Device tags pop: 'Ballad', 'Rhyme scheme aabb', 'Simile', 'Repetition', 'Humour'. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: who is truly brave, and what is the irony?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: the teased dragon saves them all, while the boastful ones hide. Real courage shows in action, not words.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: the poem is a humorous ballad with an a a b b rhyme scheme and many similes.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a dragon icon: '1. Belinda and her pets; Custard is called a coward', '2. A pirate attacks; only Custard fights', '3. True bravery is in action, not boasting'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Custard is laughed at as a cowardly dragon.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: when a pirate attacks, only Custard fights back.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: real bravery shows in action, not in boasting.

name: For Anne Gregory by W.B. Yeats

scenes.animation: A salon. Zippy holds hair dye bottles labelled 'Brown', 'Black' and 'Carrot'. A young woman with golden hair looks unsure in a mirror.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is she thinking of dyeing her gorgeous golden hair?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: To find out if anyone loves her for herself. This is For Anne Gregory, by W. B. Yeats.

scenes.animation: The poem plays out as a conversation. An older man (the poet) speaks; golden hair wraps around the woman's ears like castle walls, labelled 'honey-coloured ramparts'. A young man looks at her hair, heart-eyed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poem is a conversation between the poet and a young woman, Anne Gregory.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The poet says that young men, charmed by her honey-coloured ramparts, the hair around her ears, will never love her for herself alone.

scenes.animation: Anne holds up hair dye and colour swatches. The hair colours flip: brown, black, carrot. The young man's heart-eyes flicker.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Anne replies that she can dye her hair brown, black or carrot. Then the young men will love her for herself.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Smart move. Problem solved!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She thinks that if the colour changes, the young men will look past her hair to her true self.

scenes.animation: The poet opens an old book; a text glows with light. A caption: 'Only God could love you for yourself alone'. Anne looks thoughtful.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not quite. The poet says an old religious man found a text proving that only God can love you for yourself alone, and not your yellow hair.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The message: people are attracted by outer beauty. Only divine love looks at inner beauty.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So humans always notice looks first?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's the poet's point. He is gently telling Anne that human love is often tied to appearance.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. What does the poet mean by honey-coloured ramparts? Why does Anne want to dye her hair?' Device tags pop: 'Metaphor', 'Dialogue form', 'Rhyme'. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: what are 'honey-coloured ramparts', and why does Anne want to change her hair colour?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: explain the metaphor of her hair as a protective wall, then say she wants to be loved for her inner self.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: mention that the poem is in dialogue form between the poet and Anne.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a golden strand icon: '1. Young men love Anne's yellow hair', '2. Anne offers to dye it', '3. Only God loves for inner self'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the poet says young men will love Anne only for her beautiful hair.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Anne offers to dye her hair to be loved for herself.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: only God can love a person for their inner self alone.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Good thing I'm a spark. No hair to worry about.
